title: Players in a text file
kind: a core chapter: the log in, the register form and the Top 10 all use what you make here
one: You make a Player class that holds one player, and a PlayerFile class that reads every player from players.txt and adds new ones. A test button shows that both work.

stages.title: See how players.txt holds the players

screens.title: See what this chapter makes, and the words it uses

blocks.p: By the end of this screen, you will know what the Player and PlayerFile classes do, and why a game needs them.
Summit Ready remembers every player who registers, even after the program closes. It keeps them in a text file, `players.txt`, in the Data folder.
This chapter makes 2 classes. Player holds one player. PlayerFile reads every player from `players.txt`, checks whether a username is taken, and adds new players to the end of the file.

need: Your project from chapter 2, with the Data folder in bin\Debug (chapter 2).
The Files class from chapter 2, which finds `players.txt` (chapter 2).
About 2 hours. Your ticks are kept, so you can stop at the end of any screen and come back later.

words: while
`while` runs a loop again and again, for as long as its test is true.
not equal
`!=` means is not equal to. It is true when the two values are different.
Length
How many values a list holds, or how many letters and symbols a piece of text has.
text file
A file of plain letters and numbers, such as `players.txt`. You can open it in Notepad.
object
One thing made from a class, with its own values. Each player in the game is one Player object.
private
Only code inside the same class can use a `private` field.
constructor
The method that runs when code makes a new object with `new`. It has the same name as the class.
this
`this.username` means the field of this object, not the parameter with the same name.
property
A named value of an object that other classes can read and change, such as `Username`. It has a `get` part and a `set` part.
get
The part of a property that hands its value back to the code that asks.
set
The part of a property that changes its value.
value
Inside `set`, `value` holds whatever the code is trying to put in the property.
override
`override` swaps a method that every class already has, such as ToString, for your own one.
List
A row of values that grows as you add to it. `List<Player>` holds Player objects.
StreamReader
Reads a text file one line at a time.
StreamWriter
Writes lines to a text file.
Split
Cuts a line into parts at every bar `|`, and gives you the parts as a list of values.
foreach
Runs its lines once for every value in a list.
continue
`continue` skips the rest of the loop for this time round, and goes on to the next one.
ToLower
Gives a copy of some text in small letters, so `SummitSeeker` becomes `summitseeker`.
temporary
Only there for now. The test button is temporary: chapter 4 deletes it.
blocks.intro: You do not need to learn these words now. Where you first meet each one in the chapter, it has a dotted line under it. Hover over it or tap it to see what it means.

code.title: players.txt: the first 3 lines
partLines: The 4 parts are the username, the password, the avatar picture, and the date the player joined. The avatar is a file name from the Avatars folder.

blocks.p: A real game would never keep passwords where anyone can read them. Summit Ready does, so you can see every part of the file while you build it.
By the end of this screen, your project has a Player class with a field for each part of a line.

Each player in the game is one [[object|4]] made from the Player class. A field is a named box inside the object that holds one value. The 4 fields hold the 4 parts of the player's line. They are `private`, so only Player can change them.

code.title: PlayerFile.cs: the class and LoadAll
partLines: `static` means you never make a PlayerFile object. There is only one `players.txt`, so one PlayerFile does the job.
LoadAll gives back a `List<Player>`. It starts empty. If `players.txt` is not there, LoadAll hands back the empty list, so the game carries on with no players.
Read one line at a time

The `while` loop repeats its lines until the reader reaches the end of the file. `Split('|')` cuts each line at the bars into parts. A line without exactly 4 parts is broken, so `continue` skips it. A good line becomes a new Player, made by the second constructor, and goes into the list.
`Close` lets go of the file, so other code can open it. Then LoadAll hands back the full list.

code.title: Exists

screens.title: Check that Player and PlayerFile work

blocks.p: By the end of this screen, you know that Player and PlayerFile work, and that they skip a broken line and refuse a taken name.
Run each test with F5 and the Test button. Each test says what must not happen. If it happens, the test fails.

check.what: Click Test once, with testClimber not yet in `players.txt`.
check.how: The first message says **Added:** and shows the test player's line.
check.fix: Check Add and ToString against their yellow lines.

check.what: Close the program, press F5 again, and click Test a second time.
check.how: The first message says **testClimber is already in players.txt.** There must not be a second testClimber line, and the count stays at 13.
check.fix: Check Exists. Each name must use `ToLower()`, and `return true;` must be inside the `if`.

check.what: In btnTest_Click, change `"testClimber"` to `"TESTCLIMBER"`. Then press F5 and click Test.
check.how: TESTCLIMBER must not be added, because it is the same name in other capitals. The message says it is already there.
check.fix: Check that Exists compares both names with `ToLower()`. Change the name back to `"testClimber"` after the test.

check.what: Open `players.txt` in Notepad. Type `broken line` on a new last line and save. Then press F5 and click Test.
check.how: The program must not crash, and the count must stay at 13. LoadAll skips the broken line.

glossary: while
`while` runs a loop again and again, for as long as its test is true.
not equal
`!=` means is not equal to. It is true when the two values are different.
Length
How many values a list holds, or how many letters and symbols a piece of text has.
text file
A file of plain letters and numbers, such as `players.txt`. You can open it in Notepad.
object
One thing made from a class, with its own values. Each player in the game is one Player object.
private
Only code inside the same class can use a `private` field.
constructor
The method that runs when code makes a new object with `new`. It has the same name as the class.
this
`this.username` means the field of this object, not the parameter with the same name.
property
A named value of an object that other classes can read and change, such as `Username`. It has a `get` part and a `set` part.
get
The part of a property that hands its value back to the code that asks.
set
The part of a property that changes its value.
value
Inside `set`, `value` holds whatever the code is trying to put in the property.
override
`override` swaps a method that every class already has, such as ToString, for your own one.
List
A row of values that grows as you add to it. `List<Player>` holds Player objects.
StreamReader
Reads a text file one line at a time.
StreamWriter
Writes lines to a text file.
Split
Cuts a line into parts at every bar `|`, and gives you the parts as a list of values.
foreach
Runs its lines once for every value in a list.
continue
`continue` skips the rest of the loop for this time round, and goes on to the next one.
ToLower
Gives a copy of some text in small letters, so `SummitSeeker` becomes `summitseeker`.
temporary
Only there for now. The test button is temporary: chapter 4 deletes it.
